title: Weekly POC sync - pilot curation & rollback scenario drill
summary: Weekly pilot check-in focusing on narrowing the model catalog candidates, agreeing on a pin/rollback matrix, and drafting an emergency soft-fallback that preserves SLA. Action: Redwood to run a 10k token latency/cost sweep on candidate models and share config templates; customer to provide representative prompt sets and access to staging endpoints.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-13
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 45m
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE), Riya Patel (Redwood SE), Jonah Lee (Redwood CSM), Samir Gupta (Nimbus - ML), Laura Chen (Nimbus - Product), Marcus Ito (Nimbus - CTO), Priya Rao (Nimbus - SRE)

[00:00] Alex Morgan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check, audio ok?
[00:05] Laura Chen: Yeah all good here.
[00:12] Alex Morgan: Cool. Today a focused agenda: pick the top model candidates from the catalog, agree on pin/rollback matrix and run a drill on the fallback path. Riya will run through bench notes.
[00:22] Riya Patel: Hi folks. I pulled the three leading candidates based on the evals we ran last week - the trimmed list is: Redwood-7b-q4f, Orca-mini-8B, and Luma-13B-quant. Notation warning - sometimes the automatic transcription shows the model names weirdly in the deck, so I'll say them slowly.
[00:40] Samir Gupta: Quick question, Riya - are those the signed-off variants that include your recommended quant profiles?
[00:45] Riya Patel: Yes - for Redwood-7b-q4f it's our aggressive q4f path, Orca-mini is running 8-bit dynamic, Luma-13B has int8 channel quant. Each has different latency/cost tradeoffs which I'll summarize.
[01:10] Riya Patel: On tail latency - median token latency for the 1-2K prompt range was: Redwood-7b-q4f ~ 23ms/token, Orca-mini ~ 28ms/token, Luma-13B ~ 35ms/token on the same GPU profile. Cost per 1k tokens estimated: 7b is lowest, Orca-middle, Luma-higher. But quality varies per prompt cluster - we saw Luma handle longer context better on the product-recommend prompts.
[01:45] Laura Chen: That aligns with our internal tests - Luma gave fewer hallucinations on multi-step product reasoning. But cost matters for checkout flow where we have a budget cap.
[02:02] Marcus Ito: We care most about tail latency for in-store kiosks - 99th pct can't spike beyond 900ms or we'll break UX. What are the SLOs you can guarantee if we pin to a model?
[02:20] Alex Morgan: For Hosted API with Redwood-7b-q4f we can aim for median 20-30ms and 99th under 750ms with continuous batching on our Dedicated capacity; for Private deployments numbers shift a bit depending on infra. We can provide SLA language in the contract.
[02:48] Priya Rao: If we do Dedicated, do we get isolation for burst capacity? Last time we saw noisy neighbor issues.
[02:55] Alex Morgan: Yes, Dedicated pools are reserved. You can configure burst windows and reserve extra pods for peak - that's what most retail customers do for morning surges.
[03:10] Jonah Lee: Quick note - we've attached a short spreadsheet in the shared drive that shows the per-token cost calc for several batch sizes and sequence lengths. We'll update after Riya's 10k token sweep.
[03:25] Samir Gupta: About pinning - we want a deterministic rollback playbook. If we pin to Luma-13B for quality on recommendations, how do we ensure fast fallback to a cheaper/low-latency model if degradation occurs?
[03:40] Riya Patel: Good question. Proposed matrix: primary pinned model -> soft fallback (same family smaller variant) -> emergency hard fallback (different model with similar API). Example: Luma-13B -> Luma-7B-fast -> Redwood-7b-q4f as hard fallback. The routing rules include metadata inspection (prompt type, latency headroom) and auto-telemetry triggers.
[04:10] Laura Chen: Who triggers the switch? Automatic thresholds or manual? We need an executive signoff on auto switches.
[04:18] Alex Morgan: We recommend a hybrid: auto detection up to a staging cut (e.g., 5% traffic), then notify and pause for manual approval beyond that. For emergency only auto-cut to the hard fallback. That's customizable.
[04:35] Marcus Ito: What telemetry do we need to reliably detect regression? Latency, token error rates, quality metrics?
[04:42] Riya Patel: The minimum signals: rolling 1m 99th latency, model-specific loss triggers (we can run a small eval stream against a golden prompt set), and an uptick in query reroutes. We also recommend a lightweight semantic-quality sentinel using embeddings distance to a baseline; it's not perfect but useful early.
[05:10] Samir Gupta: Embedding sentinel sounds nice but needs to be fast. Will embedding checks add to latency cost?
[05:18] Riya Patel: Typically we run sentinel checks asynchronously on a sampled 1% of traffic. It won't add to user perception, it's just extra pipeline work.
[05:30] Priya Rao: Ops question - how do we orchestrate rollback? Is there a single control plane call or do we need to touch multiple systems?
[05:36] Riya Patel: Redwood's rollout API supports a single 'pin' call that updates routing rules across regions, and you can alias model versions. For Private, there's an operator that applies the same. We'll provide a template for the automation runbook.
[06:00] Laura Chen: Let's do a tabletop now — simulate: we detect a spike in hallucinations on checkout recommendations. What's the sequence?
[06:08] Riya Patel: Step one: auto-detect based on sentinel and quality drop. Step two: initiate a gray release - shift 10% of traffic to soft fallback and compare metrics for 10 minutes. If metric delta > threshold (pre-agreed), trigger auto-break to hard fallback and page ops.
[06:27] Samir Gupta: How fast can that 10% shift complete globally?
[06:31] Alex Morgan: Within 30s to one minute once the rollout is applied; depends on in-flight connections.
[06:36] Marcus Ito: And the rollback itself - do we need to flush KV cache? Could cached prefixes cause inconsistent outputs?
[06:43] Riya Patel: Good catch. If you rely on in-memory KV cache for long conversations, you can instruct the runtime to clear keyspaces for affected session IDs or start short-lived sessions that drop cache on switch. Our runbook will include cache invalidation steps.
[06:59] Laura Chen: For the pilot, we're worried about two failure modes: quality regressions and cost overspend. What guardrails can we set to prevent cost surprises during an emergency?
[07:10] Alex Morgan: You can set per-route caps and token budget alarms. Also autoscaling policies can be limited to a maximum number of pods and burst windows. If you hit cost alarms, the policy can auto-fallback to a cheaper model.
[07:25] Samir Gupta: Sounds good. For the next validation round, can you run a long-context 10k-token sweep across the three candidates with our prompt set? We want cost and latency per 1k token bucket.
[07:35] Riya Patel: Yes - that's what we plan. We'll run sequence-length sweeps (512, 2048, 10k) with batching simulating your traffic mix. We'll add 99th pct numbers and cost per 1k tokens.
[07:50] Jonah Lee: We'll also capture token breakdowns in the CSV - decode vs encode and KV cache hit ratio.
[08:00] Priya Rao: Regarding security - Marcus asked for audit log examples for rollback events and pin changes; can you show sample entries?
[08:06] Alex Morgan: We'll include sample audit log entries and the SAML role mapping doc in the security packet. Expect that in the packet Jonah will share after the call.
[08:20] Laura Chen: Any concerns about data residency? We need EU-only storage for specific user segments.
[08:27] Alex Morgan: We can route those segments to a EU-region Dedicated pool or Private deployment. The rollout rules support region-based routing.
[08:36] Samir Gupta: Back to the catalog comparison — can you summarize the recommended primary pin per route?
[08:42] Riya Patel: Sure. Recommendation by route: checkout/recommendation route -> Luma-13B pinned (quality), fallback Luma-7B-fast, emergency Redwood-7b-q4f. Search/summaries route -> Redwood-7b-q4f pinned for cost/latency, fallback Orca-mini, emergency Redwood-7b-q4f-older. Conversational assist -> Orca-mini pinned with a conservative token cap.
[09:10] Marcus Ito: I'd prefer fewer moving parts — do you think we can just pin two models and use a single emergency fallback? Simpler ops.
[09:18] Riya Patel: Yes two pinned per critical route is a common pattern. We suggested three to maximize safety; we'll pare it back for you if simpler is the preference.
[09:30] Laura Chen: On the evaluation metrics — how do you measure hallucination rate? We need a clear definition to automate detection.
[09:37] Riya Patel: We use a combination of exact-match checks for factual headers and a semantic recall measure against a golden set. For product data, we run entity extraction to ensure required SKUs are present. We'll share the scoring rubric in the deliverable.
[09:57] Samir Gupta: Can the rollback be scoped to a route only (not account-wide)? We have multi-tenant traffic from our partners.
[10:05] Alex Morgan: Yes you can scope by routing keys - api key, tenant id, or route path. That gives you per-tenant control.
[10:18] Jonah Lee: Small note — we'll provision unique staging API keys for Nimbus and set rate limits to mimic production but lower volumes.
[10:25] Marcus Ito: Timeline sanity check - you're proposing bench CSV by Friday (10/15), staging endpoints by 10/14, tabletop on 10/20. That fits.
[10:33] Alex Morgan: Correct. We'll also include suggested thresholds for automatic shifts for the drill.
[10:40] Priya Rao: For the staging endpoint - we'll need an IAM role and short-lived creds. Samir will share the contact for our platform infra team.
[10:48] Samir Gupta: I'll do that after the call.
[10:52] Laura Chen: Any blockers from Redwood side we should know about?
[10:55] Riya Patel: Not for the sweep; we need your prompt set and region confirmation. Otherwise we can proceed.
[11:05] Alex Morgan: Let's wrap with action items: we captured them in the notes. We'll follow up with the packet and the spreadsheet link.
[11:12] Laura Chen: Thanks everyone, appreciate the drill.
[11:15] Alex Morgan: Thanks, we'll talk soon.

End of transcript.
